clinicalPearls: COPD is defined by persistent respiratory symptoms with airflow obstruction, and the umbrella term spans emphysema (alveolar destruction with air-space enlargement), chronic bronchitis (chronic cough and phlegm), and small airway disease (narrowing and loss of small bronchioles); these coexist in varying proportions between patients.

Fixed airflow obstruction is the spirometric hallmark: a chronically reduced FEV1/FVC ratio that does not normalize after bronchodilator. The classic threshold is FEV1/FVC <0.7 (GOLD), with the ATS/ERS alternative using Z-scores of FEV1 below the lower limit of normal.

The three cardinal symptoms are cough, sputum production, and exertional dyspnea; many patients have symptoms for months to years before presenting, and a careful history often reveals respiratory symptoms preceding an apparent acute onset.

Activities involving arm work at or above shoulder level are particularly poorly tolerated, whereas activities that let the patient brace the arms and recruit accessory muscles (pushing a shopping cart, treadmill) are better tolerated.

Early disease typically has a normal physical exam; advanced disease shows prolonged expiration, wheeze, barrel chest, poor diaphragmatic excursion, accessory muscle use, the tripod posture, and cyanosis of lips/nail beds.
Digital clubbing is NOT a feature of COPD; its appearance should trigger a search for another cause, most commonly lung cancer in this population.
The blood eosinophil count (on CBC with differential) is used to guide therapy aimed at reducing exacerbation risk; an elevated hematocrit suggests chronic hypoxemia.

Chest CT is the definitive test for establishing presence, pattern, and distribution of emphysema and for medium/large airway disease; chest x-ray may be consistent with COPD (hyperinflation, flat diaphragm, bullae, hyperlucency) but cannot reliably make the diagnosis.

Guidelines recommend testing for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency in ALL patients with COPD or with asthma plus chronic airflow obstruction; serum alpha-1 antitrypsin level is the initial test, with PI-type determination for confirmation when levels are low.

Approximately only 1% of COPD patients have severe alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, yet it is the proven monogenic risk factor and demonstrates the powerful role of genetics in susceptibility; PiZ individuals often develop early-onset COPD, accelerated by smoking.
The strongest single predictor of future exacerbations is a prior exacerbation, and the single greatest risk factor for hospitalization with an exacerbation is a history of previous hospitalization.
The BODE index (Body mass index, airflow Obstruction, Dyspnea, Exercise capacity by 6-minute walk) predicts mortality better than FEV1 alone.
harrison.pathophysiology: Chronic inhaled exposures (most commonly cigarette smoke, also biomass fuels, and increasingly vaping/inhaled cannabis) in genetically susceptible individuals trigger inflammatory and immune cell recruitment in large and small airways and terminal air spaces. Large-airway changes (mucus gland enlargement, goblet cell hyperplasia, squamous metaplasia) produce cough and sputum and define chronic bronchitis. Small airways (<=2 mm) are the major site of increased airflow resistance, narrowed by goblet cell metaplasia replacing surfactant-secreting club cells, smooth-muscle hypertrophy, fibrosis, mucus, edema, and cellular infiltration; small-airway narrowing and drop-out precede emphysematous destruction. Emphysema results from a four-step paradigm: inflammatory/immune recruitment; proteinase release damaging extracellular matrix; oxidant-induced structural cell death, cellular senescence and proteolytic loss of cell-matrix attachments; and disordered repair of elastin. The elastase:antielastase imbalance (epitomized by alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency permitting unopposed neutrophil elastase) plus matrix metalloproteinases (notably MMP12) degrade elastin and collagen, generating chemotactic fragments that fuel a positive-feedback inflammatory loop. Oxidative stress (with NRF2 and SOD3 implicated, and oxidant inactivation of HDAC2 unleashing NF-kB-driven transcription of MMPs, IL-8, TNF-alpha) and impaired macrophage clearance of apoptotic cells and bacteria contribute. Physiologically, airflow obstruction with air trapping causes hyperinflation (raised residual volume, RV/TLC, and total lung capacity); a flattened diaphragm becomes mechanically inefficient. Ventilation-perfusion mismatch accounts for essentially all of the reduction in PaO2 (shunt is minimal), explaining why modest supplemental oxygen corrects hypoxemia. Inflammation can persist even after smoking cessation in susceptible individuals.
additionalDifferentials: Asthma (substantial overlap in older patients; both feature airway hyperresponsiveness and may share genetic/environmental factors)
Lung cancer (especially when new clubbing appears)
Tuberculosis-associated chronic airflow limitation (important in absence of tobacco history)
infectionMimics: Pneumonia (frequently found on imaging during presumed exacerbation)
Tuberculosis (can produce chronic airflow limitation with emphysematous and fibrotic change and airway remodeling)
HIV-associated emphysema/COPD (increased risk with lower CD4 counts; often underdiagnosed)
nonInfectiousMimics: Pulmonary embolism (incidence increased during exacerbations; should be considered)
Pneumothorax (asymmetric chest findings can mimic an exacerbation)
additionalInvestigations: Post-bronchodilator spirometry (FEV1, FVC, FEV1/FVC) for diagnosis and severity grading (GOLD vs ATS/ERS Z-scores)
Lung volumes (TLC, FRC, RV, RV/TLC) and diffusing capacity (DLCO) - DLCO reduced in emphysema
Arterial blood gas and oximetry for resting/exertional hypoxemia, alveolar ventilation and acid-base status (key in exacerbation assessment)
Complete blood count with differential (blood eosinophil count; hematocrit for chronic hypoxemia)
Chest CT (definitive for emphysema pattern/distribution, airway disease, coexisting ILD/bronchiectasis; annual low-dose CT for lung cancer screening in eligible smokers)
Serum alpha-1 antitrypsin level with PI-type determination (isoelectric focusing, mass spectrometry/genotyping, or DNA sequencing) when low
6-minute walk distance for exercise capacity and BODE index
C-reactive protein (incorporated into proposed objective criteria for staging exacerbation severity)
redFlags: New digital clubbing - investigate for lung cancer, not attributable to COPD
Respiratory acidosis with hypercarbia (PaCO2 >45 mmHg) signaling acute ventilatory failure
Mental status changes (confusion, sleepiness), inability to speak in full sentences, paradoxical abdominal wall motion
Tachycardia, tachypnea, accessory muscle use, perioral/peripheral cyanosis
Cachexia with significant weight loss (independent poor prognostic factor)
Signs of cor pulmonale / right heart failure (lower extremity edema, persistent activity limitation)
harrison.prognosis: Risk of death from COPD is closely tied to reduced FEV1 and the presence of emphysema. Mortality is predicted better by the multidimensional BODE index than by FEV1 alone. The absolute annual loss of FEV1 is highest in mild COPD and lowest in very severe disease. Cachexia/wasting is an independent poor prognostic factor. Smoking cessation slows the rate of FEV1 decline (greatest benefit when earlier) and improves survival. Among survival-improving interventions are smoking cessation, long-term oxygen in chronically hypoxemic patients, and lung volume reduction surgery in selected emphysema patients. Patients with PRISm (preserved ratio-impaired spirometry) physiology carry increased risk of mortality and respiratory and cardiovascular events. Exacerbations are episodic acute worsenings (usually <14 days) that increase in frequency as obstruction worsens (severe obstruction with FEV1 <50% predicted averages 1-3 episodes per year) and account for most COPD-related health-care costs; there is currently no cure except lung transplantation.
pitfalls: Chest x-ray cannot reliably diagnose COPD or establish chronicity; do not rely on it to confirm emphysema.
Pulmonary function testing during an exacerbation has not been shown helpful in diagnosis or management (unlike in asthma exacerbations).
Smokers with normal spirometry are not necessarily spared - many have reduced quality of life, reduced exercise capacity, emphysema/airway disease on CT, and may have exacerbations (pre-COPD).
Attributing new clubbing to COPD itself - it is not a feature and warrants a cancer workup.
Failing to test for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency in COPD patients, missing a treatable genetic cause; only a small minority of the ~1 in 3000 with severe deficiency in the US have been identified.
Overlooking pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, heart failure, or pneumothorax during a presumed exacerbation (about 25% of x-rays in moderate/severe distress are abnormal).
Underestimating viral causes of exacerbations - PCR studies show viruses may cause >50% of exacerbations.
Race-specific reference equations for pulmonary function may be inappropriate; race-neutral interpretation may be preferable.
harrison.severityClassification: Spirometric severity of airflow obstruction (GOLD, post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.7): Mild FEV1 >=80% predicted; Moderate FEV1 50 to <80%; Severe FEV1 30 to <50%; Very severe FEV1 <30% predicted. ATS/ERS alternative uses FEV1/FVC < lower limit of normal with FEV1 Z-scores (borderline zFEV1 > -1.645; mild -1.65 to -2.5; moderate -2.51 to -4; severe < -4.1). The GOLD ABE assessment additionally incorporates respiratory symptom burden (mMRC dyspnea scale or COPD Assessment Test) and annual exacerbation frequency to guide therapy. Multidimensional BODE index (BMI, obstruction, dyspnea, exercise capacity) is used for prognosis. Ventilatory failure is defined as PaCO2 >45 mmHg, classified as acute (with acidemia) or chronic by arterial pH.
management: Smoking cessation and elimination of harmful inhalational exposures as the single most effective intervention to slow disease progression
Inhaled long-acting bronchodilators (a long-acting beta-agonist plus a long-acting muscarinic antagonist), adding an inhaled corticosteroid for eosinophilic or exacerbation-prone phenotypes
Pulmonary rehabilitation and physical reconditioning to improve dyspnoea, exercise tolerance and quality of life
Immunisation against influenza and pneumococcal disease, with other routine respiratory vaccinations, to reduce exacerbations
Long-term oxygen therapy for chronic resting hypoxaemia to improve survival
Structured exacerbation treatment with intensified bronchodilators, systemic corticosteroids, antibiotics when indicated and non-invasive ventilation for hypercapnic respiratory failure
Alpha-1 antitrypsin augmentation for proven deficiency, with lung volume reduction or transplantation considered in selected advanced disease
Add-on roflumilast or a macrolide such as azithromycin for frequent exacerbators, plus nutritional support for cachexia
